summary: Defines managed objects for managing BGP-4 using network management protocols. It fixes errors introduced when the original MIB was converted to SMIv2 and updates references. It documents deployed implementations in a historical context, notes where the MIB fails to represent BGP fully, and replaces RFC 1269 and RFC 1657.

eli5.summary: A dashboard with standard gauges for a routing system. This memo defines what each gauge is called and how to read it.

subtitle: The standard SNMP objects for watching BGP-4 peers and the paths they advertise, cleaned up from earlier versions.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard set of SNMP objects to manage BGP-4 routers. The earlier BGP MIB, RFC 1657, had errors introduced when it was converted to SMIv2, including broken notifications.
tldr.mechanism: The BGP4-MIB defines a few global scalars, a peer table with state, timers and counters per BGP peer, and a table of received path attributes, plus notifications for peers entering the established state or falling back.
tldr.outcome: It fixes the conversion errors, adds compliance information and notes where the MIB cannot fully represent BGP. It obsoletes RFC 1269 and RFC 1657.

today: RFC 4273 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1269 and RFC 1657, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says work was in progress to replace this MIB module with a new one.

sections.title: Purpose and Origin
sections.content:
RFC 4273 defines the BGP4-MIB, a MIB module for managing the Border Gateway Protocol Version 4 or lower. It originated in RFC 1269, which covered BGP version 3, and was updated to BGP-4 in RFC 1657. This memo fixes errors introduced when the module was converted to SMIv2 and updates references to the current SNMP framework documents.

The abstract is candid about its aim: it documents deployed implementations in a historical context, clarifies some items, and notes errors where the module fails to fully represent BGP. It also says work was in progress to replace this module with a new one representing the current state of the protocol and its extensions.
sections.eli5: This is a tidied-up copy of an older dashboard for BGP routers. It fixes mistakes that crept in last time and admits what the dashboard still cannot show.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
Apart from a few system-wide scalars, the module has three tables. The BGP Peer Table holds information about the state and current activity of connections with BGP peers. The BGP Received Path Attribute Table holds path attributes received from peers running BGP version 3 or less, and is marked obsolete. The BGP-4 Received Path Attribute Table holds path attributes received from BGP-4 peers.

The attributes actually used to choose a route are a subset of the received attribute tables, after local routing policy has been applied. The global scalars are bgpVersion (a bit vector of supported BGP versions), bgpLocalAs and bgpIdentifier.
sections.eli5: There are three lists: one about each neighbor router, and two about the roads those neighbors told us about. The list for very old roads is marked as no longer used.

sections.title: The BGP Peer Table
sections.content:
Each row of bgpPeerTable describes one peer connection and is indexed by bgpPeerRemoteAddr. It carries the peer's state, the local and remote addresses and TCP ports, the remote autonomous system number from the OPEN message, and the BGP identifier of the peer. The identifier MUST be 0.0.0.0 unless the state is openconfirm or established, and the negotiated version MUST be zero in the same circumstances.

Counters record UPDATE messages in and out, total messages in and out, and the number of times the state machine entered the established state. bgpPeerLastError is a two-byte string whose first byte is the error code and second byte the subcode, and is zero if no error has occurred. bgpPeerInUpdateElapsedTime shows seconds since the last UPDATE was received.

The one read-write control is bgpPeerAdminStatus. Changing it from stop to start generates the BGP Manual Start Event, and from start to stop generates the Manual Stop Event, so it can restart peer connections. The RFC warns to take care about giving write access to it without adequate authentication.
sections.eli5: Each neighbor router gets one row, like a card in a file box. The card says who the neighbor is, whether you are talking, how many notes you swapped and what went wrong last time.

sections.title: Peer States
sections.content: bgpPeerState reports the connection state of the BGP finite state machine as one of six values, with the reference pointing to the BGP specification in RFC 4271. The notifications in this MIB are tied to those states: one fires when the machine enters the established state, and one fires when it moves from a higher numbered state to a lower numbered one.
sections.eli5: Making friends with another router has steps, from not talking at all up to fully chatting. The state says which step you are on.

sections.title: Timers
sections.content:
Several peer objects expose BGP timers in seconds. The configured hold time is placed in the OPEN message sent to the peer. The effective bgpPeerHoldTime is the smaller of the configured value and the Hold Time received in the peer's OPEN message. It must be at least three seconds if it is not zero, and it MUST be zero if the Hold Timer has not been established or if the configured value is zero.

bgpPeerKeepAlive is calculated so that its proportion to the hold time matches the proportion of the configured values. A reasonable maximum for the configured keepalive is one third of the configured hold time, and a value of zero means no periodic KEEPALIVE messages are sent once the connection is established. The suggested values are listed in the table below.
sections.eli5: Routers send tiny hello messages every so often to prove they are still there. If a neighbor goes quiet for too long, the router decides it is gone. These settings control how often and how long.

sections.title: Received Path Attributes
sections.content:
The BGP-4 path attribute table has one entry per path to a network, indexed by the destination prefix, the prefix length and the peer. Its columns include the origin (igp, egp or incomplete), the AS path, the next hop, bgp4PathAttrMultiExitDisc, bgp4PathAttrLocalPref, the aggregator AS and address, a locally calculated preference, whether the route was chosen as best, and any unknown attributes.

The AS path is encoded as a sequence of segments, each a type, a length and a list of AS numbers as pairs of octets. Type 1 is AS_SET (unordered) and type 2 is AS_SEQUENCE (ordered). The object also lists Known Issues: confederations produce a type of 3 or 4, and an AS path longer than 255 octets can be truncated. The multi-exit discriminator and the preference values are signed 32-bit objects, while the BGP specification uses unsigned 32-bit numbers, so they cannot represent the full range. A value of -1 means the attribute is absent.

bgp4PathAttrAtomicAggregate is lessSpecificRouteNotSelected when the ATOMIC_AGGREGATE attribute is present and lessSpecificRouteSelected when it is missing, and the RFC notes the attribute is now primarily informational.
sections.eli5: For every place you can reach, this list records which road a neighbor offered, the towns it passes through and whether it was the road you picked. It is honest that a few things cannot fit in the boxes.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
Two notifications are current. bgpEstablishedNotification is generated when the BGP state machine enters the established state, and bgpBackwardTransNotification is generated when it moves from a higher numbered state to a lower numbered one. Each carries bgpPeerRemoteAddr, bgpPeerLastError and bgpPeerState.

RFC 1657 had wrongly placed the traps under { bgp 7 } and removed bgpPeerRemoteAddr from their objects. Those older bgpEstablished and bgpBackwardTransition traps are deprecated, and the new definitions restore the semantics from RFC 1269. Implementing notifications is completely optional under the compliance statement.
sections.eli5: A notification is a doorbell. One rings when a neighbor becomes a working friend, and one rings when a friendship slips backward.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the MIB relates to inter-domain routing, improper manipulation of its objects may deny service to a large number of end users. The RFC lists the sensitive read-write objects: bgpPeerAdminStatus, where a change from start to stop can disrupt connectivity to the portions of the Internet reached via that peer, and bgpPeerConnectRetryInterval, where a bad value can keep connections down for extremely long periods.

Misconfiguring the configured hold time or keepalive can make sessions more fragile against denial of service attacks. Misconfiguring the two minimum interval objects may harm global convergence and cause long-lived routing loops and blackholes. Peer addresses can also be sensitive for ISPs. As in RFC 4113, the RFC recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: These dials can turn off real connections for many people, so only trusted people should be allowed to turn them, and the readings should be kept private.
